extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers in theoretical computer science
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic exposition of the P versus NP question: informal motivation, formal definitions (P, NP, reductions), NP-completeness, related complexity classes, consequences, and known barriers to proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of P
rubrics_metrics.description: P is the set of decision problems solvable on a deterministic sequential machine in time polynomial in the size of the input. Formally: P = {L : L = L(M) for some deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine M}, where a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine halts on all inputs and there exists k ∈ N such that T_M(n) ∈ O(n^k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the requirement that the machine halts on all inputs and the running-time bound is expressed in big-O notation; used as the formal notion of 'quickly solvable' in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of NP (verifier/certificate characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: NP is the set of languages that have a polynomial-time verifier: L ∈ NP iff there exists a binary relation R ⊂ Σ*×Σ* and k such that x ∈ L ⇔ ∃y with (x,y)∈R and |y| ∈ O(|x|^k), and the language L_R = {x#y : (x,y)∈R} is decidable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes 'quickly verifiable' via certificates y of polynomial length and a polynomial-time deterministic verifier for (x,y). The article also notes the equivalent nondeterministic Turing machine definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision problem takes as input a string w over an alphabet Σ and outputs 'yes' or 'no'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P and NP are classes of decision problems; many definitions and reductions are stated in terms of languages (sets of strings) corresponding to decision problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial-time many-one reduction (≤_p)
rubrics_metrics.description: L' ≤_p L iff there exists f: Σ* → Σ* such that for all w, (w ∈ L' ⇔ f(w) ∈ L) and there exists a polynomial-time Turing machine that halts with f(w) on its tape on any input w.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard polynomial-time mapping reduction used to relate problems; the article uses it as the formal notion when defining NP-completeness and NP-hardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: NP-completeness (two-condition definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A language L is NP-complete if and only if: (1) L ∈ NP; and (2) every L' in NP is polynomial-time reducible to L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, it suffices to show L ∈ NP and that some known NP-complete problem reduces to L. The Cook–Levin theorem establishes SAT as NP-complete and anchors many further reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: NP-hard definition
rubrics_metrics.description: NP-hard problems are those at least as hard as NP problems; i.e., all NP problems can be reduced (in polynomial time) to them. NP-hard problems need not be in NP (they need not have solutions verifiable in polynomial time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to classify problems that are at least as difficult as NP-complete problems; distinction from NP-complete (membership in NP) is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to prove NP-completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Common way: show L ∈ NP, and demonstrate a polynomial-time reduction from a known NP-complete problem to L (i.e., reduce a known NP-complete problem to the candidate), establishing L is NP-complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that after Cook–Levin, proof by reduction became the simpler, standard way to show many problems are NP-complete (example: reducing SAT to generalized Sudoku).

rubrics_metrics.name: EXPTIME and EXPTIME-complete
rubrics_metrics.description: EXPTIME is the set of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in time O(2^{p(n)}) for some polynomial p(n). A decision problem is EXPTIME-complete if it is in EXPTIME and every problem in EXPTIME has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time-hierarchy theorem implies P ≠ EXPTIME, so EXPTIME-complete problems are outside P. Examples and consequences (e.g., perfect-strategy chess on an N×N board) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: #P and #P-complete
rubrics_metrics.description: #P is the class of counting problems corresponding to counting the number of solutions (e.g., 'How many solutions exist?'); a #P problem must be at least as hard as the corresponding NP problem. #P-complete problems are the hardest in #P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that counting can be harder than decision (a #P problem gives decision information), and that many #P problems are believed to be intractable.

rubrics_metrics.name: NP-intermediate (Ladner's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P ≠ NP, then there exist problems in NP that are neither in P nor NP-complete; such problems are called NP-intermediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples believed to be NP-intermediate include graph isomorphism, discrete logarithm, and integer factorization; the article notes consequences (e.g., if graph isomorphism were NP-complete the polynomial hierarchy would collapse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifier/certificate length and verifier language L_R requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For L ∈ NP there must be a certificate y of polynomial length |y| ∈ O(|x|^k) and a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine that decides L_R = {x#y : (x,y)∈R}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This spells out both the bound on certificate size and the need for a polynomial-time deterministic decider for the relation; it's the constructive content of the NP definition used in reductions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to proofs: relativizing proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Relativizing proofs are those that remain valid in worlds with arbitrary oracles. Baker, Gill, and Solovay showed there exist oracles relative to which P = NP and oracles relative to which P ≠ NP, so relativizing techniques cannot resolve P vs NP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a formal limitation on a large class of classical techniques; the article explains the oracle model and why relativizing arguments are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to proofs: natural proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural proofs (Razborov & Rudich) are a class of circuit lower-bound techniques; Razborov and Rudich showed that if one-way functions exist then natural proofs cannot distinguish P from NP in the required way, making natural proofs unlikely to resolve P ≠ NP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes natural proofs as a barrier for circuit-complexity approaches and explains the connection to cryptographic one-way functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to proofs: algebrizing proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebrizing proofs extend relativizing techniques with algebraic oracle access; Aaronson and Wigderson showed that arithmetization-based techniques (used successfully elsewhere) also fall short — they 'algebrize' and so are insufficient to resolve P vs NP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is another formal limitation on families of proof techniques; the article presents it alongside relativization and natural proofs to explain why new approaches may be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levin's semi-algorithm illustrating accepting vs deciding
rubrics_metrics.description: Levin's algorithm (sketched) accepts the NP-complete language SUBSET-SUM and runs in polynomial time on 'yes' instances iff P = NP; it tries programs systematically and halts with 'yes' if it finds a polynomial-time program that outputs a correct solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an example distinguishing an algorithm that 'accepts' (gives yes quickly for yes-instances) from a polynomial-time decider; highlights that acceptance in polynomial time on yes-instances does not suffice to be in P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive complexity characterizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical characterizations: languages in P are expressible in first-order logic with a least fixed-point operator (FO + LFP) over ordered finite structures; NP is expressible in existential second-order logic (ESO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an alternative, logic-based lens on P vs NP; the article notes equivalences (e.g., P = NP iff P = PH) and uses descriptive complexity to restate the question in logical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for cryptography if P = NP
rubrics_metrics.description: If P = NP and the proof yields efficient constructive algorithms for NP-complete problems, many cryptosystems (public-key crypto, symmetric ciphers like AES/3DES, cryptographic hashing and blockchain constructions) would be broken because problems assumed hard would be solvable in polynomial time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cautions that a nonconstructive proof or a polynomial with impractically large constants might not immediately endanger cryptography; it distinguishes practical efficiency from formal polynomial-time bounds.
